# Gas laws (pressure, volume, temperature) (`gas_laws`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs atmospheric_pressure; helped by air_pump_vacuum, thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Air is springy. At constant temperature, halving the volume of a trapped gas doubles its pressure (pressure times volume stays constant). At constant pressure a gas expands by 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C for every degree, to a good approximation for dilute gases, which points to an absolute zero at about −273 °C. The demonstration is a J-shaped glass tube closed at the short end: pour mercury into the long arm and measure how the trapped air shrinks as the column grows; 76 cm of extra mercury halves it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting that the outside air pressure adds to the mercury column.
  - Not waiting for the gas to cool after compressing it; compression heats it and spoils the reading.
  - Applying the laws to steam that is condensing or to very high pressures.
  - Crediting Boyle alone: Power and Towneley found the relation first, Hooke built the apparatus, and Mariotte found it independently.
- History: europe: 1661–1662 Boyle (with Hooke; Power and Towneley's data); 1676 Mariotte; 1702 Amontons, pressure and temperature; 1787 Charles (unpublished) and 1802 Gay-Lussac, expansion with heat; 1834 Clapeyron combines them; 1848 Kelvin's absolute scale
- Read:
  - Robert Boyle, A Defence of the Doctrine Touching the Spring and Weight of the Air (1662)
  - Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985)
